steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
By the time the storm rolled in, Elias had already done everything he could think to do.

The lantern room gleamed—brass polished, glass wiped clear of salt and fingerprints, wicks trimmed tight and true. The afternoon’s routine checks were marked off in his logbook with his usual stiff, narrow handwriting: fuel level, lens rotation, fog signal, barometer. The last entry, made three hours ago, read:

Barometer falling. Wind veering east. Swell heavy.  
Expect foul weather by nightfall.

Now it was nightfall.

The sea had vanished behind the thick, black curtain of rain. When the lightning flashed, its brief, ghostly light showed him row upon row of angry water shouldering in from the horizon, their tops torn to foam by the wind. The lantern glass thrummed in its frame, a faint, musical vibration beneath the deeper shudder of waves striking stone. The whole lighthouse, from the iron door at its base to the weather vane on its pinnacle, seemed to flex and resist with each gust—an old, weary animal bracing itself against another beating.

Elias set a hand against the central shaft and felt the mechanism’s heart beating through the iron. Tick-click, tick-click, the escapement released the great pedestal in tiny, precise increments, turning the Fresnel lens in a slow, continuous rotation. Every eight seconds, the light swept wide across the ocean, burning through rain and spray, a briefly opened eye in the darkness.

Eight seconds of blindness for the ships out there. Eight seconds of sight.

He had always thought there was a kind of cruelty in that.

“Steady on,” he muttered to the tower, or perhaps to himself. His voice was swallowed before it could travel far; the wind made a hollow roar around the glass, like blood rushing in great, stormy ears.

He checked the clock fastened by a leather strap to the brickwork. A little after ten. He would make his eight-bell rounds as he always did—storm or not, end of the world or not. Ritual was what kept the shape of things. Without it, hours turned amorphous and heavy; his mind, too.

Down the iron steps he went, the spiral narrowing as it plunged, boots sending faint metallic notes down the well. He passed the landing with the radio—silent, as it had been for the past week. Passed the landing with his little kitchen—lamp burning low, kettle on, the blue mug he always used turned upside down on the table to keep the dust out, although there was never any dust up here, only fine salt that sneaked through every crack. Passed the landing with his bunk and the single porthole that stared inland, toward a darkness that was—if anything—even deeper, for there were no other lights along this stretch of coast. Only dunes and heather and, further still, the dim suggestions of hills.

At the base, he opened the iron door a cautious inch. Wind knifed through, instantly plastering his shirt to his ribs. He let the door slam again and put his shoulder against it until the latch caught.

No need to go outside tonight. No one would be walking the cliffs. No one sane.

He worked his way back up to the service room, where the fuel drums were kept, and ran his hand along their dented sides. Enough oil for another month, at least. He uncapped the main feed and peered into the dim meniscus. Still plenty. The emergency canisters were stacked neatly under the bench, their brass caps lined up like soldiers. All as it should be.

He ticked items off on his fingers: lamp—good. Lens—clean. Clockwork—running. Fog horn—primed, though the storm served as its own warning. Fuel—sufficient. Windows—latched. Logbook—updated.

There was really nothing left to do.

Elias went back up to the lantern room and stood with his back against the cool brick, eyes half-closed, listening to the sea. The rotation of the lens cast slow-moving bars of light and shadow across his worn face and the thin knit of his jersey. Every revolution, the hotter side of the lamp passed close, bringing with it a wash of dry heat that threatened to close his eyes for good.

He had not always been alone.

Before the light was automated everywhere but here—before budgets and men in suits declared that an electric bulb on a timer could do what a keeper did—there had been a crew of three. In those days the tower was full of voices: arguments over card games, muttered gossip over tea, the occasional burst of a song. The sound had seeped into the stone, he thought. Sometimes, when the weather was calm and the sea polite and flat as slate, he fancied he could still hear them in the walls, laughter echoing faintly like trapped birds.

Before that, before the navy, before the war that had put white in his beard and a stiffness in his left knee that flared in damp weather, there had been an entirely different life. A little house inland. A woman who hummed by the window when she sewed. A little boy with hair the color of storm foam, of spindrift caught in sunlight. He remembered the boy’s hand in his own: small, sticky from jam, the trust in the way the fingers curled around his thumb.

The house was gone now. The woman lay under a stone with ivy creeping along its base. The boy had grown into a man, and the man had written from another coastline far to the south to say that city lights needed him, that there was no place for him among the gulls and waves. That he was sorry. That he would visit when he could.

He had not visited in three years.

Elias’ hand drifted, by habit, to the inner pocket of his jacket. The envelope there was softening at the corners from repeated handling. He did not open it. He knew the words by heart. Just the touch of it reassured him: the last trace of that other life, a line flung from shore to shore, thinner than one of the cobwebs that formed in the tower’s corners when he let his cleaning slip.

The light swung, slow as a heartbeat. Out over the dark, over the unseen teeth of the submerged rocks, over the place where, in better weather, you could sometimes make out the freighters as smudges of moving gray against the horizon.

He tried to imagine them now. Men on decks slick with rain, engines straining, radar screens glowing green in the gloom. Did any of them spare a thought for the man in the tower whose light kept them from grinding their hulls to steel splinters? Did any of them look up through the streaming glass of the wheelhouse and say, That’s Gannet Point. Old Elias keeps that one. Good fellow. Never misses a night.

Of course not. Perhaps the captain, once in a while, would note the flash pattern and murmur something appreciative about the reliability of the service, in the same tone one admired the predictability of the tide table or the accuracy of a watch.

Reliability. That was what a lighthouse keeper was. Not a person, not really. An extension of the stone. Part of the mechanism.

Again the bar of light swept past, etching the lines on his hands in stark relief. The knuckles swollen with age. The left ring finger bare.

He startled at the sound of the radio.

It was only a crackle at first, a dry cough from the speaker down on the second landing. He frowned and went down, boots ringing on the metal treads, heart picking up speed in a way that annoyed him. Fool, he scolded himself. It will only be static. Or some fool boy at the harbor club playing with the wireless for a laugh.

The set glowed faintly green, its tuning dial hovering just off center. Elias eased himself into the chair beside it and lifted the microphone, listening.

“—annet—oint Light— repeat, this is the fishing vessel *Martha Anne* calling Gannet Point Light.”

The voice was thin, stretched over distance and weather, but unmistakably real.

He swallowed a dry thickness from his throat, thumbed the transmitter button. “*Martha Anne*, this is Gannet Point. Receiving you. Go ahead.”

“Thank God. We’re about eight miles east-southeast of you, bearing for the harbor, but the GPS is—” a burst of static, “—gone blind. Radar’s a washout in this rain. I can just make out your light when we crest, but we need a fix. Our skipper says he doesn’t like the look of the swell by the headland. Can you give us a line, over?”

Elias leaned forward, suddenly sharp. Eight miles, east-southeast. In this weather, with faulty instruments, it would be easy to veer too close inshore. Those unseen teeth waited just under the surface, ready to chew the bottom out of any boat foolish enough to wander over them.

He pulled the chart from its drawer with a practiced hand, spread it on the desk, pinned the corners with two mugs and a folded wrench. His fingers moved with a memory older than his aches, drawing compass arcs, plotting.

“What’s your last confirmed position?” he asked.

They gave it. He marked it, drew a line toward the harbor mouth—a wide, generous line, accounting for current and the likely drift of a tired crew in a rising storm. He noted the time. The speed they claimed they were making.

“When you see the beam, count,” he said. “From the moment it comes dead over your bow. Count out loud. Can you do that, *Martha Anne*?”

“Aye, Gannet Point. Standing by. Over.”

He sat with the microphone in his hand, listening to the hiss and snap of the ether. His other hand rested gently on the side of the chart, feeling the faint texture of the paper beneath his fingertips. The tower shuddered as a stronger wave broke against its base. Somewhere below, a loose tool rattled against stone.

Then:

“Light dead ahead. Mark. One… two… three…”

The voice on the radio counted. Far away, his own light spun, inhumanly regular. Eight seconds of sight. Eight seconds of dark.

“—eight.”

“Again,” Elias said. His eyes, though lined and red at the edges, were clear. He watched the little clock on the shelf, listened for the faint change in the mechanical whirr above that told him the lamp was facing due east.

They did it twice more. The times matched well enough. He made his marks, corrected for drift, for the push of the heavy swell from the southeast. His pencil stabbed the chart with more force than was strictly needed.

“You’re coming in too close,” he said. The words were flat, steady. “You need to steer ten degrees further out to sea. Ten degrees starboard. Hold that for twenty minutes, then adjust back. That’ll put you clear of the Rookery Reef. You understand?”

There was a brief silence, during which he could hear muttering, the background clank and sway of a ship under strain.

“Understood, Gannet Point. Ten degrees starboard, twenty minutes. Much obliged.” A pause, lighter now. “How’s the view from up in your palace this evening?”

Elias allowed himself the smallest of smiles. “Wet,” he said. “And dark. Same as yours.”

A low chuckle came over the speaker. “Can’t argue with that. Save us a cup of tea, will you? Over.”

“I’ll put the kettle on,” he said automatically. “Over and out.”

He set the microphone down gently. For a moment, he simply sat, listening to the ticking of the clock and the deeper, slower tick-click of the lamp above. He traced the route he had given them with his fingertip—a curve that slid out, away from danger, then in, toward the safe, narrow slit of the harbor mouth between its two breakwaters.

The kettle, he realized, was already on. He had left it there out of habit before starting his rounds. With slow care, he rose, went down the steps to the kitchen landing. The lamp’s yellow light made the small space feel almost cozy, in defiance of the storm’s hollering outside. He lifted the kettle; it clucked, half-boiled. He added more coal to the stove, then moved through the familiar motions of spooning tea leaves into the infuser, setting out his mug.

He hesitated, then took down another mug from the shelf. It had been his son’s once, years ago—a chipped thing with a faded painting of a trawler on it. He placed it beside his own.

Steam feathered against the low ceiling. The lighthouse moaned as another gust hit it broadside.

He poured, carefully, into both cups.

Back in the lantern room, he watched. Leaning on the narrow sill, his face close to the cold pane, he peered into the blackness until his eyes watered. He could see nothing but the swirling gray of rain in the sweep of his own light.

Still, he watched.

From time to time, he went down to the radio and listened. Once he heard the fishing boat again: voices more relaxed now, talking of catching the green marker buoy that told them they were on the right path. The skipper—the same voice as before, though with an ease that came from land drawing near—came on to say thank you, proper this time.

“Couldn’t have done it without you, Gannet Point. Would’ve run right up on those bloody rocks if not for your eye up there.”

“Just doing my job,” Elias said.

“Best job I’ve ever heard of,” the man replied. “Stay dry, friend.”

The radio crackled, then stilled.

He did not know their faces. They would not know his, if they passed him later in the village. To them, he was nothing more than a steady voice, a reference on a chart. Gannet Point. Flash every eight seconds. Elevation one hundred and twenty-seven feet.

It was enough.

He went back up to the lantern and, with an old sailor’s eye, shifted his gaze inland, to where he knew the harbor lay though he could not see it. Somewhere over there, deck boots were clanging on wet metal, ropes were being made fast, men were stepping onto solid ground with the small, unspoken gratitude that followed any rough passage safely ended. Maybe one of them, shaking rain from his cap, would say, That was a nasty one. Lucky the light was on tonight.

Snow had once fallen this time of year, when he was a boy. He remembered watching it from a different window, the flakes soft and fat in the glow of town lamps. Here, on the cliff, the first chill of winter always came as rain, fine and needling, then heavier, until the whole sky seemed to empty itself in one furious weeping.

The storm went on.

Midnight came and went. He made more tea. He wound the weight that drove the lamp, muscles in his back twinging as he took the strain of the winch handle. He checked the oil again. He wrote in the log:

2135 hrs. *Martha Anne* called. Visibility poor. Provided navigational assistance. Vessel reported clear of Rookery Reef, entering harbor at approx. 2220 hrs. No further incidents.

He paused before the last three words, pen hovering.

No casualties.

There. That was better. Record it properly. This was how you kept the shape of things.

Between duties, between trips up and down the spiral, his thoughts wandered—to the boy in the city, to the envelope in his pocket. He imagined a different storm, in streets between glass towers, rain chasing itself in lines down vertical planes. His son hurrying beneath an umbrella, shoulders hunched, face turned away from the weather. Did he think of this place, ever? Did the memory of salt wind and gull cries cut across the exhaust and sirens? Or had the city soundtracked his life so completely that the sea had become a story, a thing that happened to other people?

On some nights, when the loneliness pressed too insistently at his ribs, Elias took out paper and wrote. Little, practical letters: The light is in good order. The storms this year have been bad. I fixed the rain gutter. I think of you, lad. Come when you can.

He never sent them. They joined the others in a small tin box under his bunk, held down with an elastic band. Words, coiled and unsaid.

Tonight, he did not write. Tonight, his hands were full with the work that had called him away from that other life in the first place: the slow, constant tending of a flame.

Outside, slowly, the wind began to lose its edge. The roar softened to a steady, tired rush. The thunder moved out to sea, lightning flickering as a faint, far-off pulse instead of a violent, white stab.

By four in the morning, the rain had eased to a patter. The clouds were still thick, but something in their bellies had changed. The pressure on his ears eased. The barometer, when he checked it, showed the needle arrested in its fall.

He climbed one last time to the top, joints muttering. His breath fogged the glass. The sea was visible now as a sheen of dark metal, bruised here and there by the ghostly paleness of breaking waves. The horizon, a slightly lighter band. No ships. Somewhere beyond his line of sight, the *Martha Anne* lay snug against her berth, her hull knocking gently against wooden piles.

He rested his fingertips against the glass directly in front of the light. The warmth seeped in, faint but real.

“Good enough,” he said softly. To the lamp. To the tower. To himself.

Dawn came almost shyly, as if embarrassed to be seen after such a chaotic night. The eastern sky blushed from black to deep indigo, then to the bruised purple of an old plum. A thin, pale strip of gold appeared, widening, diffusing. The first gulls wheeled and cried, their silhouettes scribbled briefly across his windows.

He turned off the lamp.

For a moment, the absence of its hum was shocking. The silence lay on his ears like a blanket. Without the slow movement of the lens, the room felt smaller, somehow, as if the great eye had closed and left him in a more intimate dark.

He descended the stairs into the lighthouse, which suddenly seemed full of its own small noises: the creak of timber, the settling tics of stone contracting as the outer air warmed, the distant slosh of residual waves against the rock.

In the kitchen, he poured out the dregs of last night’s tea and rinsed the mugs. He paused when he reached the chipped one, thumb rubbing once over the faded trawler. Then he set it carefully, mouth down, beside his own.

The radio crackled.

He glanced at it, surprised. Dawn was usually a quiet time. The traffic came in bursts—bursts of hurry, of work, of deadlines—later, when harbors woke and people stepped onto desks and bridges and streets.

He toggled the switch.

“Gannet Point Light, this is Harbor Control. Do you read, over?”

“Reading,” he said. “Go ahead.”
